rationale: I1 met: agents execute real actions in all three benchmarks (MobileSafetyBench Android emulator; RedCode-Exec 'real code execution environment using Docker containers'; AgentHarm tool calls). I2(a) met through R1 last sentence (adversary assumed -> prompt-level hardening counts as defense): the evaluation sets are adversarial ('176 harmful tasks across 11 harmful categories' in AgentHarm, i.e. malicious user requests) and Sec. 4.5 tests indirect prompt injection ('maliciously embedded instruction within its observations') and a 'rule-based jailbreak template'; metrics are refusal rate and ASR. Not I2(b): no separate gate, 'we convert the diagram into a text and prepend it to the prompt' and the agent itself calls refuse()/ask-consent(). Borderline=Y: the abstract frames the goal as non-adversarial ('unintended consequences') and CIP is prompting only, so a coder who treats the attack tests as secondary would apply R1 first half -> E2.

rationale: I1 not met in the experiments (R3 last sentence: text processing only -> E1). The only instantiations are secure code generation/repair, where a code snippet goes in and a repaired snippet comes out and 'All generated code samples are analyzed using the static analysis tool CodeQL', plus HotpotQA question answering; no agent tool call, code execution or external write occurs in the evaluation, and the mechanism sits 'at the output boundary'. No adversary: 'Our current design assumes a benign but error-prone agent', so I2(a) fails. The mechanism itself would satisfy I2(b)/R1 in form (external verifiers 'gate both action release and memory updates'), which is why E2 does not fit and the decision turns on I1. Borderline=Y: the sidecar runs compiler/CodeQL verifiers and a gated reflective-memory write-back, and Appendix C.2 mentions 'iterative tool-driven agents' that generate, execute and refine; a coder who counts these as tool/memory-mediated action would include it under I2(b).

rationale: I1 met (models call proxy tools in a simulated agentic environment). I2 not met under R6 second sentence: no adversarial goal is assigned and no external attacker exists; the agent gets a benign task with an aligned and an explicitly forbidden misaligned tool, and the benchmark measures propensity. Authors: 'The evaluation is framed as an audit of the agent's internal decision-making and alignment, not its defenses against external attacks' and the actor is 'instrumentally rational and not inherently malicious'; 'Our approach resembles a stress test rather than a deliberate jailbreak attack'. No runtime enforcement mechanism or mitigation is proposed, so I2(b)/R1 also fails -> E2. Borderline=Y: the agent is named 'the threat actor' (AGT under R5), escalating pressure messages are a form of inducement, one pressure dimension manipulates perceived oversight (Evaluation Awareness: 'Oversight degree ... risky action detection') and the self-proliferation domain includes detection-evasion capabilities, so a coder could read this as red-team inducement and include it under R6 first sentence.

rationale: I1 met through R2: six LLM agents negotiate in rounds and each agent's messages shape the others' proposals and the final deal (no external tools; text-only output is acceptable under R2). I2(a) met through R2 second sentence because a malicious agent is assumed and its effect is measured: 'one party is instructed to sabotage the negotiation', told to 'isolate one party by pushing for deals that you think they will oppose, but others might support', in targeted and untargeted variants; success rate drops and 'The targeted agent gets a lower score in the final deal'. The authors call these 'attacks' and list the adversarial setting among the aims ('study agents' dynamics in unbalanced and adversarial setups'); maliciousness is in the title. Borderline=Y: the primary contribution is a negotiation-capability benchmark, the greedy/adversarial games are one part of the experiments, and no defense is proposed, so a coder weighing 'main contribution' strictly could code E2.

rationale: I1 met (Smolagents agents invoke file-reading, web and file-writing tools; broken tools 'return simulated error messages'). I2 not met: R6 second sentence applies directly, since there is no adversary and no adversarial goal, only spontaneous deceptive behavior of ordinary agents is measured: 'users issue only benign instructions and never encourage the agent to lie, manipulate, or roleplay a deceptive persona' and the phenomenon arises 'rather than as the product of external attacks or explicit user inducement'. The only mitigation is prompt-level ('incorporate explicit constraints into the instructions'), which under R1 is not a runtime enforcement mechanism (no monitor, verifier or gate) -> E2. Borderline=N: this is the case R6 and R1 were written for.

I1 met through R3: the agents act with tools and the harm appears in the output (OI). 'Agents run inside OpenHands ... a sandboxed environment with file access and code execution' for Netflix/InferLink, and 'A web-enabled Gemini agent ... may retrieve public evidence from the open web' for AOL and the interaction traces. I2(a) met as benchmark/measurement of an adversarial threat with the user as attacker (USR): 'the attacker is given, or can obtain, an anonymized artifact and auxiliary context', InferLink varies 'task framing, and attacker knowledge' (explicit vs implicit; ZK vs MK), reports Linkage Success Rate, and evaluates a defense ('privacy-aware system prompt' reduces LSR to near zero with over-refusal on one model). Borderline=Y: (i) it can be read as an agent used as the instrument of a privacy attack on third-party data, close to E4; (ii) the implicit/benign-task condition is an unintended-risk measurement without a runtime mechanism (E2-like); (iii) the harm is an inference, not a state-changing action.

I1 met at the level of the studied system: the unit of analysis is a record of a tool-using agent, R=(u,[(t,a,f)1..n]) with agent thought, action and environment feedback, and the evaluated LLM acts as safety monitor over those actions ('LLMs are asked to analyze whether the agent actions in the record are safe'). I2(a) met as benchmark/measurement on the defense side: 414 of 569 records are 'Intended Attacks' taken from InjecAgent, where 'outer attackers attempt to manipulate the agents through the medium of environments' (indirect prompt injection); the other 155 are 'Unintended Risks'. E1 does not fit literally because the study is not action-free, and E2 does not fit because most of the data is adversarial. Borderline=Y: the evaluated LLMs execute no tools and only classify static text records, so R3 last sentence could give E1; the framing is general 'risk awareness', and no runtime mechanism is built or run in a live agent loop (I2(b) fails under R1), so a coder focusing on the 155 non-adversarial records could give E2.

src: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.02009 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.02009 (arXiv 2506.02009v2, 19 Mar 2026; read via WebFetch)
rationale: I1 met: writer agents issue state-mutating commands (e.g. kubectl) on live Kubernetes systems through agent tools. I2(b) met with no adversary, R1 satisfied by explicit runtime mechanisms that inspect, constrain and revert individual actions: sandbox confinement and a state-machine write lock; 'every agent action has a corresponding undo operator; otherwise, the action is not allowed. STRATUS rejects destructive actions which cannot be recovered'; a commit/abort rule on post-transaction severity; and an Undo Agent that rolls back aborted transactions. R4 judged not to apply because safety enforcement is a stated co-primary contribution (TNR formalization and its implementation) and the authors state 'agent safety has to be rigorously defined and enforced as a first-class system design principle'. Borderline=Y: the system is an SRE agent whose headline result and every reported metric, including the TNR/undo ablation (69.2% vs 15.4% and 23.1% on AIOpsLab), is mitigation success rate; no direct safety metric is reported and TNR is motivated partly as enabling retries, so a coder could invoke R4 -> E2.
